title: AI Browser Extensions in 2026: Install These, Skip Those
body_md:
Screenshot of layerxsecurity.com (source)

My view: AI browser extensions deserve more scrutiny than they usually get. I'd be most comfortable with extensions from vendors I already trust and pay, such as Claude in Chrome, and I'd review any "free AI sidebar," "GPT summarizer," or unfamiliar agentic assistant before keeping it: check the publisher, the privacy policy, and the permissions it requests, and remove it if you can't justify them. In LayerX's enterprise data, AI extensions had higher rates of known vulnerabilities and broader permissions than extensions overall, and a free tool with no clear business model can fund itself through your data. ## What's Actually Going On

Screenshot of go.layerxsecurity.com (source)

### AI extensions are now mainstream - and measurably riskier than everything else in your browser This isn't a vibes-based warning. LayerX's Enterprise Browser Extension Security Report 2026, published April 10 and drawn from browser extension usage across more than 1 million enterprise devices, found that 99% of enterprise users have at least one extension installed, about 25% have more than 10, and about 15% have an AI extension installed. The risk delta is the part that should stop you. About 10.8% of all extensions contained a vulnerability with an assigned CVE, compared with 16.31% for AI extensions - that's 51% higher by those two numbers, though LayerX's own summary rounds the gap to 60%. AI extensions were three times more likely to request cookie access, with 18.19% of them doing so, and 2.5x more likely to be able to execute remote scripts. Then there's drift. 34% of all extensions increased their permissions in the past 12 months, and AI extensions were 6 times more likely to have done so. An extension you vetted in January may not be asking for the same things in September. And the paper trail is thin: LayerX's report put the share of enterprise-used extensions with any privacy policy at 28.6%. ### The attack surface isn't theoretical - 2026 gave us the receipts Microsoft warned in 2026 that malicious AI assistant extensions were impersonating legitimate AI tools and harvesting LLM chat histories and browsing data, including full URLs and chat content from platforms like ChatGPT and DeepSeek. Reporting cited approximately 900,000 installs, and Microsoft Defender telemetry confirmed activity across more than 20,000 enterprise tenants (Microsoft Security Blog, March 2026). The Cloud Security Alliance's April 2026 research note makes the uncomfortable point that those installs accumulated because employees pick AI extensions based on store ratings, peer recommendations and marketing claims - and unlike SaaS apps that go through procurement review, extensions install with one click and start touching sensitive data immediately. CSA also flags an earlier case: in July 2025, Urban VPN Proxy quietly shipped code in version 5.5.0 that intercepted AI conversations across eight major platforms. Why is this so easy? Because of what extensions structurally *are*. Palo Alto's Unit 42 lays it out plainly: extensions run inside the browser's trusted process and can read and modify web content, intercept network requests, access cookies and talk to external servers. Worse, a hostile extension can route traffic through attacker infrastructure or attach the Chrome Debugger Protocol to read decrypted HTTPS response bodies. HTTPS doesn't save you from something living inside the browser. ### Meanwhile, the platforms are absorbing the useful features anyway Separate from security, a second reason for skepticism is redundancy: browsers are adding the same features themselves. Google wired Gemini 3 into Chrome on January 28, 2026, with a side panel and an agentic feature called auto browse. The new Gemini in Chrome is available on Windows, MacOS and Chromebook Plus in the U.S., and auto browse is rolling out in preview in the U.S. for Google AI Pro and Google AI Ultra subscribers (Google). The standalone-browser bet already claimed a casualty. OpenAI announced Atlas's retirement in July 2026, and the company deprecated it, moving browser-based agentic capabilities into ChatGPT and Codex; Atlas stopped working on August 9, 2026. The counterexample - and it matters - is Anthropic's extension. Claude in Chrome is an extension for paid Claude plans, and its Chrome Web Store listing displayed about 17 million users in early October 2026. It's an add-on for paying users. An extension tied to a subscription, from a vendor with a reputation to lose, is a reasonable model, though not a guarantee of safety. ## Sorting the Useful From the Risky

Screenshot of unit42.paloaltonetworks.com (source)

I think some "best AI extensions" roundups get this backwards. They rank by feature list - summarize a page, rewrite an email, compare prices - as if those features were scarce. They aren't. Page summarization is increasingly built into browsers themselves. Accepting broad permissions such as cookie access for a feature your browser already offers is a poor trade. Here's my rule of thumb, an opinion rather than a guarantee: **prefer AI extensions from vendors you already pay and trust, and review permissions before installing any.** Claude in Chrome makes sense if you pay Anthropic. Grammarly may make sense if you write for a living; it offers a free plan and paid plans (see its plans page), and its extension needs the same permission review. A paid subscription gives a vendor revenue other than your data, though it is not a security control. A free extension from an unfamiliar developer still has to fund itself somehow. To the skeptic who says I'm fearmongering: LayerX's data actually undercuts the lazy version of this argument. AI extensions were *more* likely to be actively maintained than non-AI ones - only 22% unmaintained, versus 40% of extensions overall. The problem isn't abandonware. It's live, actively-updated software with escalating permissions and a direct data pipe to third-party LLM providers. That's a harder problem than "delete the old stuff." A second point: "AI extension" is not one category. A grammar checker that reads your text box and an agentic assistant that clicks buttons in your logged-in banking tab are not remotely the same risk. LayerX's own recommendation is that these shouldn't be treated the same as a simple spell-checker, given their elevated permissions, faster rate of change, and direct access to sensitive in-browser data. Agree completely - and I'd go further. I'd avoid letting an agent act without confirmation in a session where money, identity, or account recovery is reachable. ## The Strongest Counterargument

Screenshot of labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org (source)

The best case against me: gatekeeping by subscription is a proxy, not a security control. Big vendors ship CVEs too, paid products get breached, and "only install from companies you pay" conveniently entrenches the incumbents while smothering genuinely better small tools. There are useful niche extensions - research clippers, transcript exporters - built by small teams that may never offer a paid plan. My rule filters those out along with the junk. That's a real cost, and I won't pretend otherwise. I still land where I land, because the asymmetry is brutal. The CSA research note argues that installs like those of the 900,000-install impersonation campaign accumulate because people judge extensions by store ratings and peer recommendations - the exact signals a good indie tool and a malicious clone both display. Until there's a trust signal a normal person can verify in a minute, "do I pay this company" is a crude filter: better than none, not a guarantee. ## Bottom Line If you install extensions casually, do this today: open your extensions page, remove any AI extension you don't recognize or no longer use, and check the publisher and permissions of the rest. Before adding anything new, read the permission prompt. If it wants to read and change data on all sites, plus cookies, for a feature your browser already has, think twice. Microsoft's guidance is likewise to review installed extensions and remove unknown ones. If you manage a team, treat extensions as software that can reach production data rather than as a personal preference, and inventory them. The people who should care most are anyone whose browser holds client data, financial dashboards, or customer records. ## FAQ **Are AI browser extensions safe to use at all?** It depends on the publisher and the permissions requested. The category-level numbers are a reason for caution: 16.31% of AI extensions carry a known CVE versus about 10.8% of extensions overall. Sticking to vendors you know and pay reduces risk but doesn't remove it, so still review permissions. **Do I still need an AI extension if my browser has AI built in?** Often not. Chrome now has a Gemini side panel, and auto browse is available to AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in the U.S. as a preview. Summarize-and-rewrite extensions overlap heavily with what's already there. **Is ChatGPT Atlas still an option?** No. Atlas shut down on August 9, 2026. Treat any comparison article still ranking it as out of date. **What's the single biggest red flag when installing one?** Permission creep. 34% of all extensions increased their permissions in the past 12 months, and AI extensions were 6 times more likely to have done so - so audit quarterly, not just at install. *Updated October 2026: this post is based on published vendor documentation and security research, not on hands-on testing of the extensions discussed; figures I couldn't verify in a primary source have been removed.* ## My Take My read is that the interesting shift in 2026 wasn't a new threat, it was a new default. Chrome ships Gemini in the side panel; ChatGPT's capabilities moved into an app and an extension from a company with lawyers. The marginal "free AI sidebar" from a developer you've never heard of is now competing with a built-in feature, which means the only way it gets installed is by promising something your browser won't do - usually more access, not less. So I think the install bar should go up, not down. Specifically: if an extension asks for cookie access or the ability to run scripts on every site, I want a reason beyond "it's convenient," and I want to know who's on the hook if it misbehaves. The LayerX permission-creep number is what makes this ongoing rather than one-time - the thing you approved is not necessarily the thing running next quarter. The fair point against me is that paying a vendor buys accountability, not security. Anthropic, Google and Grammarly can all ship a vulnerable build, and 16.3% CVE rates include plenty of extensions from companies with real revenue. My rule is a filter on incentives, not on code quality, and I'd rather say that out loud than dress it up as a security control. I'm not a security professional, and nothing here is a substitute for advice from one - especially if you're deciding policy for a team. What I'd watch next is whether browser vendors start surfacing permission *changes* as loudly as they surface the initial install prompt. Until they do, the audit is on you, and the only version of it that works is the one you actually put on the calendar.
